_doc: The AUTHORED half of the terrain for epoch e1834_harbor_cut at the forks. generators/terrain_gen.py reads this plus river.geojson and hydrology.geojson and writes heightfield.json + heightfield.bin + the terrain GLBs. Every elevation here traces to a numbered zone in docs/research/01-terrain-hydrology.md; nothing is invented to make the ground interesting. Elevations are in FEET above the summer-1835 lake and river water surface (the internal datum, data/datum.json) and are converted to metres at generation.
scope: The forks quadrant: the Chicago River main stem, North Branch and South Branch meeting at the datum origin at Wolf Point, and the three divisions of land they separate.
critical_caveat: No contour survey of the 1835 town site exists. The earliest systematic levels are the 1850s street-grade and Chesbrough sewerage surveys. Every land elevation below is a period narrative statement in feet, back-calculated from grade-raising records, or inferred from geology — so NO land elevation in this spec is better than 'inferred', and the generator refuses to emit a 'documented' confidence for any land vertex. The one documented surface is the water: the pre-reversal river was sluggish and outward-flowing with a near-zero surface gradient, standing at lake level through the whole downtown reach.

grid.note: 641 m square centred on the datum origin, 2.5 m cells (8.2 ft — inside docs/PLAN.md's 5-10 ft), quantised at 5 mm, which is 1/15 of the 0.25 ft the dossier asks for. Row 0 is the SOUTH edge and column 0 the WEST edge, matching the renderer's Heightfield sampler.

vertical.datum: Z = 0.0 ft at the summer-1835 lake and river water surface
vertical.exaggeration_note: 1.0 and it stays 1.0 in the data. Total natural relief inside this box is under 6 ft. A vertical-exaggeration control may exist in a renderer, labelled, defaulting off — see docs/LIBERTIES.md L3.

water.mesh_note: The water surface is the plane Z = 0 by the definition of this project's vertical datum, and terrain_gen.py emits it at a literal zero rather than reading this figure. So the mesh says exactly what this value says and does not say it BECAUSE of this value: change the 0.0 here and nothing moves. It is recorded because the datum has to be stated somewhere a reader meets it. The agreement is checked rather than trusted: terrain_inputs.RESTATES holds this figure against water_surface_m in the heightfield the bake wrote, converted from feet, so editing it fails the gate instead of quietly telling a visitor the river stands somewhere the ground does not.
water.note: Flat: the water surface is treated as lake level throughout the downtown reach and the river gradient as zero. WHAT ACTUALLY HOLDS THIS UP IS WEAKER THAN THE GRADE SAYS, and the honest statement of it belongs where a visitor reads the claim. No source read by this project measures the river's surface gradient. The sentence this `documented` rests on is one line of unfootnoted encyclopedia prose about sluggish pre-reversal flow, written in a section about the 1900 reversal. The regrade to `inferred` is queued rather than taken because a confidence is a mesh input and it lands with a Blender bake — docs/ROADMAP.md § S5, docs/STATUS.md § 45. THE PERIOD WITNESS IS DELIBERATELY NOT CITED HERE. Swearingen stood on this bank in August 1803 and wrote that the river was 'dead water' — but in the same clause he gives the cause, 'owing to its being stopped up at the mouth, by the washing of sand, from the lakes', which is the closed-mouth regime this project models as the epoch e1830_natural. This scene is e1834_harbor_cut: the bar is cut and the mouth is open, so his observation describes the condition that was removed. Attaching a tier-1 source to a claim it does not make would be over-grading dressed as a citation. See docs/RESEARCH/swearingen_1803.md § 5.

reaches.note: Dossier zone 20 gives the main-stem thalweg at -12 to -18 ft, with the -18 ft pool at the fort bend 1.2 miles downstream. The shallow end of that range is used here because the forks are the upstream end of the reach. Swearingen's 1803 sounding of 'upwards of 18 feet' is a measurement AT THE FORT and is not carried up to the forks. As of 2026-08-11 that sounding is cited from the journal itself rather than from a paraphrase of it: quaife_1913_swearingen, Appendix I, pp. 376-377. The note above described a source this block did not cite, which is the fault it was written to warn about, one level down.
Dossier zone 21 gives -6 to -10 ft for the branch beds above the forks, itself inferred. Midpoint taken. No sounding of either branch was located.

channel_profile.shape: depth = bed_ft * (1 - exp(-d_in / e_fold_m)), d_in = distance from the waterline into the channel
channel_profile.e_fold_note: The e-folding distance is the river's. A watercourse may override it: the north-side slough is 7 m wide, and a 9 m e-fold would make a 1 ft channel 4 in deep and invisible.
channel_profile.mesh_note: The formula is written out here for a reader and implemented in terrain_gen.py, which does not read the string. The mesh does what this line says, and what holds the two together is one step weaker than a comparison: prose cannot be compared to Python, so terrain_inputs.RESTATES names the generator's own line and the gate requires it to still be there, exactly once, with comments stripped. A reformat fails it, which is the right way round — the sentence and the line are meant to move together.
channel_profile.note: The cross-section shape is a smooth approach to the reach bed and carries no evidence at all — no cross-section of the Chicago River at the forks exists for any date before dredging. It is under water and invisible; it is here so that the surface reaches Z=0 exactly at the traced bank line and so a boat draught question has an answer. Marked conjectural in the confidence channel.

bank.profile: ease_out_quadratic: h = level * (1 - (1 - d/face)^2), steepest at the waterline
bank.note: Horizontal distance over which the ground rises from the waterline to the local near-river level. 6 m is what a natural low bank in river alluvium looks like at a 2-4 ft rise; no source gives a bank profile at the forks. The resulting crest sits at each division's near_ft below, which is what implements dossier zone 13 (+2 to +4 ft at the forks). ONE PERIOD WITNESS BEARS ON THIS AND HE IS CITED FOR EXACTLY WHAT HE SAYS. Swearingen, arriving 17 August 1803, measured the fort bank at about 8 ft and then wrote of the reach upstream — the reach this box models — that 'the banks above are quite low'. That is corroboration of a low bank from a man who was looking at it, and it is the only sentence in his Chicago passage that reaches this quadrant. It carries no number, so it cannot promote the grade and does not: this stays conjectural, because the 6 m profile and the 2-4 ft rise are still ours. Added 2026-08-11; before that this block cited nothing at all. See docs/RESEARCH/swearingen_1803.md § 5.
bank.mesh_note: As with the channel section: the ease-out is implemented in terrain_gen.py rather than read from this string, and the ramp line it describes is named in terrain_inputs.RESTATES and required to still be in the generator. face_m is the figure that shapes the bank, and it is read.

divisions.label: South Division — the plain west of State Street
divisions.note: The plain west of State Street 'sloped down to the river in a level plain elevated only two to three feet above the river'. State Street is roughly 840 m east of the origin, so the whole South Division inside this box is that plain. The rise from 2.4 ft at the bank to 2.9 ft at 300 m inland is 0.15 ft of fall across a 300 ft chord — inside the dossier's flatness rule of 0.5 ft per 300-ft block. Marked inferred, not documented: the source is a secondary synthesis that gives no citation for the figure and no survey underlies it.
divisions.mesh_note: range_ft is the dossier's stated span and near_ft/far_ft are the figures picked out of it, which are what the generator reads. bank_crest_ft restates the crest the bank ramp arrives at: the ramp multiplies the division level and reaches 1.0 at the top of the face, so the crest IS near_ft. The two carried the same number by hand and this note used to say that nothing checked they still would. Something does now — the figure is declared restated_in_code and terrain_inputs.RESTATES names near_ft as the half it has to match.

divisions.label: North Division — timbered, better-drained sandy ground
divisions.note: Zone 19 gives the North Division +4 to +7 ft, rising toward the lake; zone 13 gives the bank crest at the forks +2 to +4 ft and says the ground rises slightly on the timbered north side. Reconciled as a 3.6 ft bank crest rising to 4.6 ft at 300 m inland — 0.31 ft of fall across a 300 ft chord, inside the flatness rule with room for the micro-relief on top. The North Side is documented as carrying a thrifty heavy growth of timber, which is consistent with better-drained sandy ground.
divisions.mesh_note: As south_division: the span is the dossier's, the two picked figures are the build instruction, and the crest restates near_ft — which is now a declaration the gate holds the pair to rather than a sentence.

divisions.label: West Division — Wolf Point and the open wet prairie
divisions.note: Zone 18 gives the West Division wet prairie +3 to +6 ft with 1-2 ft slough swales; zone 13 caps the bank at the point at +2 to +4 ft. Reconciled as 3.2 ft at the bank rising to 4.3 ft at 300 m — 0.34 ft of fall across a 300 ft chord, inside the flatness rule with room for the micro-relief on top. The West Side is documented as open prairie entirely free from timber.

marsh_strips.note: The South Division was 'generally low and marshy ground', with 'a strip along the river shore that was still more marshy, where land and water mingled, covered with tall grass, reeds and rushes'. Dossier zone 11 puts that strip 40-120 ft back from the bank at +0.5 to +2.0 ft. 30 m (98 ft) at +1.25 ft is the middle of both ranges. Applied only to the South Division shore because that is the division the source names; the north and west shores get the plain bank profile instead. This is what makes the bank a crest rather than a ramp: the ground behind it is LOWER than the bank top, which is the natural-levee form a low alluvial bank takes.

swales.note: Zone 18 says the West Division wet prairie carried 1-2 ft slough swales. That they existed is inferred from the dossier; WHERE they ran is not attested anywhere and this alignment is invented. Kept shallow (0.75 ft over a 30 m half-width, about 2.3 ft per 300 ft) and recorded as a liberty in docs/LIBERTIES.md.

watercourses.note: Existence and course documented by Wright 1834; width measured off the drafted band; depth invented. A shallow, still, connected backwater is the form the sources describe for sloughs off the Main Branch: 'marshy, wet areas with little current'.

micro_relief.applies_to: land above the waterline, faded out across the bank face
micro_relief.mesh_note: Where the noise applies is decided in terrain_gen.py — it multiplies the bank ramp, which is zero at the waterline — and this line describes that rather than driving it. terrain_inputs.RESTATES names the assembly line that does it, so moving the noise outside the ramp fails the gate rather than leaving this sentence describing ground the model no longer has.
micro_relief.note: Two octaves of value noise at +/- 0.10 ft (30 mm) — below the 0.25 ft the dossier asks the heightmap to be quantised at, and far below the resolution of any statement in the record. It exists so that a surface the sources describe as dead flat still reads as ground rather than as a rendering error, and so that walking gives motion parallax. It is a texture, not a claim. Set amplitude_ft to 0 for a perfectly flat plain.

surface_materials.mesh_note: Nothing in the model is made of this. The ground mesh carries one surface for the whole box — the renderer's earth colour — so the profile a visitor reads here, under the strongest confidence grade this project awards, is a statement about the site and not a description of the surface in front of them. What a soil section would change if it were built is the colour and texture of the ground, and neither is driven by this value.
As south_division: one earth colour covers the whole box and no surface material is modelled.
surface_materials.note: The profile itself — about a foot of black loam over three to four feet of saturated fine sand over eight to twelve feet of impervious blue clay — is stated for the BUSINESS DISTRICT, which is the South Division plain south of the main stem. Carrying it across the river is the dossier's own grouping of zones 8, 9, 18 and 19 under one entry (docs/research/01-terrain-hydrology.md, surface-material table), not a second observation, so this is inferred where the south_division entry is documented. Against it: the same dossier describes the North Division (zone 19) as timbered, better-drained sandy ground, which is not what the loam-over-quicksand-over-clay section describes. Nothing reached measures a section here.

surface_materials.mesh_note: As south_division: one earth colour covers the whole box and no surface material is modelled.
surface_materials.note: Inferred by the same extension as the north_division entry: the profile is stated for the business district and the dossier's surface-material table groups zones 8, 9, 18 and 19 under it. Two things weaken it here and are recorded rather than resolved. The dossier's own stratigraphic list maps the wet prairie west of the South Branch to the Equality Formation (lacustrine silt and clay), which is a different surface unit from the loam-over-sand-over-clay section; and the West Division is the one zone in this box whose ground is described as wet prairie carrying slough swales rather than as town ground. The grouping is followed because it is the statement that assigns zones, and the disagreement inside one report is the reason this is not documented.

surface_materials.mesh_note: The marsh strip IS in the ground — it is the dip behind the bank crest — but what it is made of is not: peat, sedge, reeds and rushes are the flora and surface parcel (S6), and the strip renders in the same earth as the plain behind it.

The note below has said since this entry was written that nothing in the renderer is coloured from it. That sentence is a declaration now, checked against what the generator reads, and it holds for the other four entries too — which no sentence said.
surface_materials.note: Nobody in this project has seen this bed and no source record here describes it. The Cahokia Alluvium is the unit modern geological mapping puts along the river margins of this region, and the dossier assigns it to the channel zones (20-21 and the abandoned southward channel) on that basis, tagging the assignment inferred itself (docs/research/01-terrain-hydrology.md, surface-material table; the mapping it rests on is a modern geology reference and is not among data/sources/). It is a formation name carried onto this reach by regional mapping, not an observation of the Chicago River bed in 1835 — which is why it is inferred and not documented, and why nothing in the renderer is coloured from it.

vegetation_note: For the flora parcel, not implemented here: the West Side is documented as open prairie entirely free from timber; the South Side carried a body of timber along the river extending east as far as Wells Street; the North Side a thrifty heavy growth of timber; the river banks sedgy grass and abundant wild onions (chicagology_prefire273).

not_modelled_in_this_box.why: the lakeshore sand-ridge belt is on the Michigan Avenue line, about 1.4 km east of the origin
the Fort Dearborn mound is about 1.2 km east
the State Street break-of-slope is about 840 m east
the slough from the public-square pond enters the river at the foot of State Street, about 840 m east
the public-square pond is at Randolph/Washington and Clark/LaSalle, about 550 m east
the Frog Pond at Lake and LaSalle is about 480 m east
the Wells Street marsh is about 600 m east
the 1834 cut through the bar is at the river mouth, about 1.6 km east
